claims.text: CoCrFeNiTa_x high-entropy alloys can exhibit FCC and BCC structures.
The representative CoCrFeNiTa_x systems are considered near their fusion temperatures.
An active-learning surrogate can be trained on a limited subset of ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations.
The training calculations can faithfully include vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Active learning can selectively sample solid- and liquid-phase ab initio MD data and interpolate complete free-energy surfaces.
The proposed surrogate can capture configurational, vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration free-energy contributions.
FCC and BCC crystal structures and local atomic environments mediate the modeled phase transitions.
Increasing Ta content can produce an FCC-to-BCC structural transition in CoCrFeNiTa_x.
Strategically selecting a subset of ab initio MD calculations reduces the amount of molecular-dynamics sampling required.
Interpolation by the surrogate preserves the fidelity needed for robust phase-transition predictions.
The method will reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio MD.
The method will be significantly faster than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Predicted phase free energies and melting temperatures will agree within about 5% of explicit ab initio MD results.
Predicted specific heat will agree within about 5% of explicit ab initio MD results.
The proposed framework is applicable from elemental and binary systems through moderate- to high-complexity multicomponent alloys near fusion.
Explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD provide accurate free-energy evaluations but are especially expensive for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Accuracy may deteriorate for systems with extreme anharmonicity or electron–vibration coupling outside the training regime.
Deviation exceeding 5% from explicit ab initio MD in phase free energies or derived fusion properties across several systems would falsify the hypothesis.
